newsitem.title: INDIA: Rumoured rigging in India stocks unlikely-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rumoured rigging in India stocks unlikely-analysts.

text.p: Recent talk of price rigging on Indian stock markets was far fetched because the presence of foreign institutional investors and local funds would deter price manipulation, analysts and brokers said on Wednesday.

Recent allegations of price manipulation were triggered by a stunning share market rally in recent weeks which saw the benchmark stock index soar nearly 24 percent early in the year after a three-year bear phase.
Analysts said the surge was fuelled by government-inspired expectations of taxes and other incentives to warm up a sluggish industrial sector and revive gloomy capital markets.
"Price rigging is not feasible because the field is broad," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at brokerage Kotak Securities Ltd, the Indian associate of U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs.
He said scores of foreign institutional investors and local mutual funds would pounce on any unreasonable rise in prices to sell shares.

"In earlier years the market was vulnerable to rigging because there were fewer players," Jhaveri said. "Today, fund managers are driven by valuations -- there are so many of them that it is impossible for a group to rig prices."
But newspaper editorials said the buying, led by speculators, pointed to rigging.
"...There cannot be an instant turnaround in the market after a prolonged bear phase. It can only happen due to manipulation and rigging," The Times of India said in a recent editorial.
"The stench of bull rigging in the bourses," screamed the headline of an editorial in the Indian Express.
Analysts said the market's steep recovery was a fast correction of the sharp sell-off late last year.
"What one should be careful (of) is not to over-react," said Uday Kotak, vice chairman of finance firm Kotak Mahindra Finance.
"I think the markets are correcting themselves and the good news is that the markets are correcting themselves much faster," he said.
"If there was an element of volatility, speculation or rigging, the markets have corrected it very fast."

The top-30 share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index was trading at 3,566.61 points on Wednesday afternoon, off the January 16 intraday peak of 3,812.31 but sharply up from the three-year low of 2,713.12 touched on December 4, 1996.
"I think when the market went down to 2,700, clearly it was an over-reaction and when the turn happened, it happened too fast," Kotak said.
"We're going to see some volatility but the bottom line message is going to be we'll see steady improvement in Indian markets." he added.
